analysis.one_liner: Makes public community college tuition-free for everyone and four-year public college tuition-free for working- and middle-class students.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 68 House Democrats, never received a hearing or a vote; it was referred to three House committees in June 2023 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set up a federal-state partnership to wipe out tuition and fees for every student at community colleges and two-year tribal colleges, and for working- and middle-class students at public four-year colleges — roughly households earning up to $125,000 for a single parent or $250,000 for a married couple. It would also nearly double the maximum Pell Grant at public colleges, let students use Pell money for living costs, extend Pell eligibility to Dreamer students and students with temporary protected status, and pay private nonprofit historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions to drop tuition for eligible students. It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and no committee ever acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at community colleges — all of them, regardless of income — and working- and middle-class students at public four-year colleges, who would stop paying tuition and fees. Low-income students would also get much larger Pell Grants, usable for rent and living costs, and Dreamer students would become eligible for federal aid. States would receive most of the funding, covering 100% of the cost in the first year and phasing down to 80%.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Community college students and middle-class families

how_it_helps.text: The bill funds states and tribal colleges to eliminate tuition and required fees for all students at community colleges and two-year tribal colleges, and for working- and middle-class students at public four-year institutions.

It raises the maximum Pell Grant for the 2024-25 award year to $14,790 for students at public and tribal institutions, extends how long students can use Pell Grants (to 7 years and 6 months), and allows Pell money to pay for living and other nontuition expenses.
It expands Pell eligibility to Dreamer students and students with other immigration statuses such as DACA and temporary protected status.
It pays private nonprofit historically Black colleges and universities and minority-serving institutions to eliminate tuition and fees for students from households under the same income limits.

States receiving grants must maintain their own higher education spending, keep instruction spending per student from falling, and move toward at least 75% of instruction delivered by tenured or tenure-track faculty within five years.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through mandatory appropriations of 'such sums as may be necessary' from fiscal 2024 through 2033 — the federal share is 100% in the first year and phases down to 80% by 2028-29. Participating states must also contribute a share rising from 0% to 20%, and must maintain their existing higher education funding as a condition of receiving money.

drawbacks.text: The cost is large and open-ended: the bill directly appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' for fiscal 2024 through 2033 rather than a fixed amount, and the federal government would pay 80% of the cost after the phase-in — a permanent multi-billion-dollar annual commitment that would compete with other federal priorities.
At public four-year colleges, married-couple households earning up to $250,000 qualify for free tuition, meaning a substantial share of the benefit goes to families well above the median income.

States that join must keep their higher education funding at or above recent averages and take on a growing share of the cost, which some states could not meet in a recession — though the bill includes unemployment-triggered relief from those requirements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and concrete: free community college for everyone and tuition-free public four-year college for most families, plus a near-doubling of the Pell Grant for low-income students. The costs are also large and permanent, and the income caps let some upper-middle-class families into the program. This is a major new spending program, honestly described — the question is whether the country wants to fund it, and Congress never let that question reach a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, and no committee ever held a hearing or moved it, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on June 14, 2023, with 67 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors.
The Speaker referred it to the House Education and Workforce, Budget, and Ways and Means Committees on the day of introduction.
No committee took any further action on the bill; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The student loan industry benefits from the bill's death, since college costs — and therefore borrowing — stay where they are. Taxpayers are spared a large new mandatory spending commitment, and the status quo of high college prices persists for students and families.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan industry; taxpayers spared the cost

for.name: Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the College for All Act of 2023 on June 14, 2023.

for.name: 67 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the Education and Workforce, Budget, and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred; the bill shows no action beyond its June 14, 2023 referrals through the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 68 supporters were House Democrats and there were no Republican cosponsors; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists, and the Republican-controlled committee chairs took no action on it.

industries.note: Wiping out public tuition and nearly doubling Pell Grants would sharply reduce the need for students to borrow, shrinking the loan market. The bill's death preserves the borrowing status quo.
Public institutions would receive large per-student federal payments and gain enrollment as cost barriers fall, with strings attached on instructional spending and faculty hiring.

industries.industry: Private nonprofit HBCUs and minority-serving institutions
industries.note: The bill makes these institutions a permanent federal funding channel: they would receive grants roughly equal to $4,880-$10,200 per eligible student to eliminate tuition, with annual eligibility review. It explicitly bars recent for-profit-to-nonprofit converts from this money.
